segments.text: Meet a kirana shopkeeper. Hundreds of customers pay them by UPI every week. But if even one of those buyers was paying with stolen money, the police can ask the bank to put a hold on the shop's account. Suddenly the shopkeeper cannot use their own money, and they are asked to prove that the sale was real. Weeks have passed. There is no bill, no record of what was sold, nothing but their memory.

Other tools help a merchant write a letter after the account is frozen. Kavach makes sure the proof already exists before the freeze happens. It records what was sold at the moment of payment, tied to the payment company's own transaction records. Let us see it on four live screens: the buyer's phone on the left, the Soundbox on the shop counter, the shopkeeper's app, and the bank's console on the right. All four are connected, and each screen sees only what that person would really see.

A customer buys two kilos of sugar and a bottle of oil, for eight hundred and twenty six rupees. On their phone, the shopkeeper makes a bill with the amount and the items, and chooses: let the Soundbox ask for the payment. The bill goes straight to the Soundbox on the counter, which shows the bill's own QR code and speaks the request out loud.
कृपया 826 रुपये का भुगतान करें, दो किलो चीनी, एक तेल के लिए।

The buyer scans the QR on the Soundbox. Their payment app looks the bill up, shows the amount, and they pay with their UPI PIN. Notice what the buyer sees: only the amount and the shop. Nothing about Kavach.
एआईटीएम पर 826 रुपये प्राप्त हुए। बिल का भुगतान हो गया।

The Soundbox announces the payment, just as it does today. But behind the scenes something new has happened. The bill and the payment were joined together in the same instant the money arrived. That record is append-only: it can never be edited, and nothing can be added to it later. On the shopkeeper's app, the payment now shows its proof, and a proof strength label that tells them how much weight their records can carry.

Not every buyer waits for a bill. Some simply scan the shop's QR and pay. For those payments, the Soundbox asks the shopkeeper what was sold, and they just say it, in their own language, with a single tap on the mic. No typing. If they miss it, they can write the bill on their phone, but only within two minutes of the payment, never afterwards.

Now, the twist. Days later, the person who paid eight hundred and twenty six rupees turns out to be using stolen money. The victim calls the cyber crime helpline, and the complaint reaches the bank. Look at the shopkeeper's app and the Soundbox: they show nothing. Kavach never tips anyone off before a hold actually exists.

The bank places a lien, limited to that one payment, as the Home Ministry's procedure requires. Only now does the shopkeeper's app turn red. Instead of panic, it explains in plain Hindi: only eight hundred and twenty six rupees is on hold, not your whole account. This is a hold on one payment, not an accusation. And here is what you can do.

Before preparing any document, Kavach asks two honest questions. Did you lend your account to anyone else? Were you paid a commission to receive someone's money? A person who answers yes is not given an innocence letter. They are directed to free legal aid instead. Kavach protects honest merchants. It does not help money mules.

Our shopkeeper answers no to both. Kavach now prepares two things. First, a sale certificate. It keeps the payment company's records, the transaction, the settlement and the bill, clearly separate from the shopkeeper's own words. Second, a grievance letter to the bank. Every rule it cites comes from a verified rules table, with its source and the date it was last checked. The AI writes the words, but the facts come only from that table.

Everything is marked as a draft, not legal advice, with no guarantee of release. The shopkeeper reads it, and files it through their own bank. Kavach never sends anything on its own. Then they simply mark it as filed, and Kavach starts counting the days.

The bank has seven days to reply. The police officer has fifteen more. Let us jump ahead to day twenty two. No decision has come, so Kavach has the next letter ready: an escalation to the District Grievance Officer, again as a draft for the shopkeeper to file.

That is Kavach. Proof at the moment of sale. Verified against the payment company's own records. And delivered through the Soundbox and the app that shopkeepers already use, in their own language. Other tools write a letter after the freeze. Kavach makes sure the proof already exists before it.
